numerical_failure.observed_behavior: With use_distance=True, linear_rainbow ordered observations by Mahalanobis distance to an arbitrary middle-indexed observation (exog[nobs // 2]) and built the covariance around that single point, so the F-statistic and p-value depended on the raw row order of the data; with a constant column in exog the covariance was singular and raised a LinAlgError. Discrete lattice data with distance ties gave 69 distinct F values over 100 permutations (spread 0.17) when using argsort.
numerical_failure.expected_behavior: The statistic should be invariant to row order: Mahalanobis distances measured from the exog centroid (multivariate mean), using the pseudo-inverse of the covariance so a constant column contributes 0 and no exception is raised; ties ordered deterministically via lexsort. Continuous data over 5 permutations should give spread about 8.9e-16 (floating-point noise); discrete lattice over 100 permutations should give 1 distinct F with spread about 6.7e-16; constant-column model should give F=1.3847543113 with spread about 2.2e-16.
trigger_conditions: same data supplied in a different row order
exog contains a constant column (singular covariance)
discrete or duplicated regressors causing exact Mahalanobis distance ties

input_output_examples.input: continuous data, 5 permutations of rows, use_distance=True
input_output_examples.expected_output: spread 8.9e-16 across permutations (statistic identical up to floating-point noise)

input_output_examples.input: constant-column model (typical regression with intercept), use_distance=True

oracle_clues: Reproducer compares spread of F across row permutations against floating-point noise (about 1e-15)
Commit cites matching R's lmtest::raintest as reference behaviour
Regression tests test_rainbow_use_distance_order_invariant[False|True] assert statistic identical across permutations

numerical_characteristics.precision: Spread values of 8.9e-16, 2.2e-16 and 6.7e-16 are reported as floating-point noise for the fixed model, versus 0.17 spread before the fix (argsort), with 69 distinct F values before and 1 distinct F after across 100 permutations of the discrete lattice
numerical_characteristics.magnitude: F-statistic approximately 1.3847543113 for the constant-column model; permutation spread on the order of 1e-16 after fix versus 0.17 before
category_specific_evidence: Order invariance: the F-statistic from linear_rainbow(use_distance=True) must be identical across row permutations; for continuous data over 5 permutations spread was 8.9e-16 (floating-point noise)
Discrete integer-lattice design over 100 permutations gave 1 distinct F with spread 6.7e-16, versus 69 distinct F with spread 0.17 under argsort before the fix
Constant-column model no longer raises LinAlgError and gives F=1.3847543113 with spread 2.2e-16; the pseudo-inverse of the covariance handles the singular case

Violated property: the Mahalanobis center must be the exog multivariate mean (np.mean(exog, axis=0)), not the arbitrary observation exog[nobs // 2]; the old covariance was built around that single point, so results depended on raw row order
Ordering uses a deterministic lexsort keyed on distance (primary) and exog values (tie-break) instead of non-stable argsort, so exact distance ties do not reintroduce order dependence
Test test_rainbow_use_distance_matches_manual_ordering checks equality with ordering by Mahalanobis distance to the centroid recomputed independently
Test test_rainbow_center_deprecated: passing center emits FutureWarning and does not change the result
Existing value-asserting test_rainbow uses use_distance=False, so no reference values change
reproduction_risks: Discrete-lattice result depends on lexsort tie-breaking; using argsort reproduces the order-dependent failure
Constant-column case exercises the former LinAlgError path; a full-rank design will not reproduce it

Discussion notes a docstring/warning mismatch on center (warns only when use_distance is True), which conflicts with the stated FutureWarning-always behavior and should not be assumed as the reproduction target
Issue #9103 mentions the rainbow test being liberal under non-normal errors; this is a power/size remark and not a numerical reproduction target
